The reproductive biology of the Rufous elephant shrew (Elephantulus rufescens) is characterized by a modest litter size, with each successful pregnancy yielding a single offspring [N_R_i = each successful pregnancy yielding a single offspring]. Females in this species are capable of producing up to 5.2 litters per year [F_R_i = up to 5.2 litters per year], a remarkably high frequency for an insectivorous mammal of its body size when measured at typical active body temperatures of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]. Gestation itself lasts for 61 days [tg = 61 days], which is notably long for a mammal with such a small neonate at a temperature of 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C]. This prolonged developmental period occurs under a uterine temperature of 35.3 °C [T = 35.3 °C], slightly below the maternal core temperature, and is thought to facilitate the advanced state of neuromuscular development observed in the altricial neonate at parturition. The gestation period, when combined with the extremely high annual litter frequency, indicates a rapid post-partum return to estrus and minimal lactational anovulation in this species.

Newborn individuals are extraordinarily small relative to the adult female, with the wet weight at birth averaging just 10.6 grams [Wwb = 10.6 grams]. This exceedingly small neonatal mass, placing the newborn among the smallest relative birth weights recorded for any eutherian mammal, imposes a substantial energetic burden on the lactating female. The suckling juvenile must more than double its birth mass during the pre-weaning period to achieve a wet weight at weaning of 29 grams [Wwx = 29 grams] at the time of nutritional independence. The transition to solid food occurs at 23 days after birth [tx = 23 days after birth], a relatively short suckling period for a mammal of this adult size, measured during periods of maternal activity at 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]. This rapid weaning is likely an adaptation to the high metabolic demands of the female, allowing her to quickly resume the energetic investment required for the next reproductive cycle, as the species maintains an extremely high year-round reproductive output.

Under steady-state thermal conditions at 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C], female Rufous elephant shrews reach their ultimate wet weight at approximately 58 grams [Wwi = approximately 58 grams], though considerable individual variation exists, with adult body mass typically ranging from 25 to 60 grams depending on local resource availability and reprod(25-60 grams [Wwi = 25-60 grams]) uctive status. This asymptotic body mass is modest even by macroscelidid standards, and it constrains many physiological and life-history parameters. The pubertal milestone is reached relatively early in the species' development: the time since birth at puberty is 50 days [tp = 50 days]. at a temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]This early sexual maturation permits females to begin reproducing within a few weeks of their own weaning, a life-history strategy that maximizes lifetime reproductive output in a species with a relatively short maximum lifespan of approximately 7.9 years [am = approximately 7.9 years] at a temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C].

Comparative studies among sengi species reveal that Elephantulus rufescens exhibits an accelerated reproductive schedule relative to its congeners, driven in part by its exploitation of unpredictable food resources in East African savannahs. The maximum lifespan of approximately 2,884 days [am = approximately 2,884 days] is considerably shorter than that of the larger Petrodromus tetradactylus, suggesting a trade-off between high annual fecundity and somatic maintenance at a temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]. Under field conditions, reproductive females maintain a core body temperature near 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C] during active foraging periods, which supports the rapid metabolic processes required for producing over five litters each year. The species exhibits no pronounced breeding season in equatorial regions, with females capable of entering postpartum estrus within days of parturition. This continuous breeding strategy is energetically demanding, and recent field studies suggest that individuals in suboptimal habitats may show reduced litter frequency, though litter size remains fixed at one offspring [N_R_i = litter size remains fixed at one offspring] as a biomechanical constraint of the narrow pelvic canal in this small-bodied mammal.

The juvenile period following weaning is marked by a phase of rapid somatic growth, during which the weaned individual must nearly double its body mass to approach the lower end of the adult size range. Observations of captive colonies indicate that the age at first reproduction for females that successfully wean their own first litter aligns closely with the physical attainment of the pubertal milestone at 50 days after birth [tp = 50 days after birth] at a temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C]. This early first reproduction, facilitated by the accelerated pre-weaning development, is a key determinant of the species' high intrinsic rate of increase. As a predominantly insectivorous forager, the Rufous elephant shrew faces significant thermoregulatory challenges that influence its activity patterns; maintaining a body temperature of 37.3 °C [T = 37.3 °C] during nocturnal foraging bouts incurs substantial metabolic costs. The species' life-history syndrome, combining extreme precocial reproductive maturity, a fixed single-pup litter, and a high annual frequency of litters, represents a distinctive adaptive strategy among small-bodied mammalian insectivores inhabiting seasonally arid tropical environments.
